title: Excitonic Stark Response Induced by Quantum Capacitance in van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Xiangzhi Hong, Yongkang Jian, Yang Chen, Rukai Cang, Yuanlong Guo, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Baigeng Wang, Erfu Liu
abstract: Precise electrostatic control in van der Waals heterostructures is commonly described by a geometric capacitor model, which assumes that the internal electric field is fully determined by external gate voltages. Here, we show that this description breaks down in the presence of interfacial charge transfer, where quantum capacitance modifies the internal electrostatics. Using interlayer excitons as local probes, we observe a dipole-dependent energy splitting that persists even when the gate-induced geometric field is nominally canceled. This splitting reflects incomplete cancellation between gate- and carrier-induced fields set by quantum capacitance, while many-body renormalization is largely symmetric with respect to the two opposite dipole orientations, allowing the splitting to provide a direct optical measure of the local chemical potential. Our results reveal the central role of quantum capacitance in interface electrostatics and provide a route to probe it in operando.
summary: This research demonstrates that the simple geometric model for electrostatics in vdW heterostructures is insufficient when charge transfer occurs, as quantum capacitance modifies the internal fields. By measuring the dipole-dependent energy splitting of interlayer excitons, the authors successfully isolate and quantify the local chemical potential, establishing a direct optical diagnostic tool for interface electrostatics.
main_problem: The standard electrostatic description of van der Waals heterostructures fails when interfacial charge transfer occurs, necessitating the inclusion of quantum capacitance effects.
main_result: The dipole-dependent energy splitting of interlayer excitons provides a direct optical measure of the local chemical potential, revealing the central role of quantum capacitance in interface electrostatics.
method: The study uses interlayer excitons as sensitive optical probes to measure energy splittings, comparing results against theoretical models incorporating both geometric and quantum capacitance effects.
model_or_system: The system involves interlayer excitons in van der Waals heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/graphene) under dual-gate control. The model contrasts the simple geometric capacitor approach with one incorporating quantum capacitance ($C_Q$) due to interfacial charge transfer.
key_observables: Dipole-dependent energy splitting, energy shift dependence on external field, and the separation of Stark effect contributions from many-body screening.
important_parameters: Quantum capacitance ($C_Q$), local chemical potential ($\mu$), gate voltages ($V_{top}, V_{bot}$), and dipole orientation ($	ext{IX}\uparrow$ vs. $	ext{IX}\downarrow$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the dipole-dependent asymmetry is dominated by the residual Stark effect due to incomplete field cancellation, while the symmetric component tracks many-body screening.
figures_summary: Figures show the deviation of measured Stark shifts from geometric predictions, the near-identical behavior of binding energy variations for opposite dipoles, and the quantitative agreement between calculated residual Stark splitting using $C_Q$ and experimental measurements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the failure of the geometric model, then uses interlayer excitons to measure dipole-dependent splittings. It systematically separates the Stark effect from many-body screening, ultimately quantifying the chemical potential via the residual splitting predicted by quantum capacitance theory.
why_interesting: The work provides a novel, optically accessible method to probe the local chemical potential and the fundamental role of quantum capacitance in nanoscale device electrostatics, bridging quantum optics with condensed matter theory.
